habitat: Freshwater crocodiles (also known as 'freshies') inhabit the rivers, streams, billabongs, and freshwater wetlands of northern Australia, from the Kimberley region of Western Australia through the Northern Territory to Queensland. Unlike the larger, more dangerous saltwater crocodile, freshies prefer upstream freshwater habitats and avoid estuarine and marine environments. During dry season, they may aestivate in burrows dug into riverbanks when water bodies shrink or dry up.
diet: Freshwater crocodiles are opportunistic predators, feeding on fish, amphibians, crustaceans, aquatic insects, turtles, water birds, snakes, and small mammals. Their narrow, elongated snout — adapted for catching fast-moving fish — distinguishes them from the broad snout of the saltwater crocodile. Juveniles eat proportionally more insects and crustaceans. They hunt primarily at night using ambush techniques in shallow water.
behavior: Freshwater crocodiles are generally shy and pose minimal threat to humans — bites are extremely rare and typically occur only when the animal is harassed or accidentally stepped on. They are fast and agile both in water and on land. During the dry season, they may travel overland to find remaining water sources. Females dig hole nests in sandy riverbanks, laying 10-20 eggs. The mother does not guard the nest but returns at the time of hatching to assist juveniles to water. They are the only Australian crocodilian that readily climbs trees and rocks.
facts: Freshwater crocodiles are significantly smaller than saltwater crocodiles, typically reaching 2-3 meters (males) and 1.5-2 meters (females). Their narrow snout is an adaptation for piscivory (fish-eating), unlike the broad snout of the fish- and mammal-hunting saltwater croc. They are found in stunning freshwater gorges and billabongs across northern Australia. They can survive droughts by burrowing into mud. In Aboriginal Australian culture, the freshwater crocodile features in Dreamtime stories and traditional art.
naming: Freshwater crocodile names might reflect their Australian habitat or sleek build. Consider names like Freshie, Billabong, Darwin, Kakadu, Kimberley, Archer, Slender, Outback, Snapper, Arnhem, or Tiwi.
